new_statements.quote: Accent is not marked because it is purportedly not phonemic, although the author's statement of this is somewhat confusing: 'Word accent in Q[uezon], B[rooke's] P[oint], C[anipaan], and M[olbog] falls on one of the last two syllables of a word, including both suffixed and unsuffixed forms. . . In none of the languages are words distinguished by accent alone so accent is not contrastive on this level and is not written' (10). I interpret this to mean that some of the dialects are oxytone (regular accent on the ultima) and some are paroxytone (regular accent on the penult), a situation not unusual in Austronesian languages that have lost accent
new_statements.citation: Thiessen, Henry Arnold. 1981. Phonological reconstruction of Proto-Palawan. Anthropological Papers 10. Manila: National Museum, p. 10 -- as quoted in Zorc, R. David. [1983c, publ. 1984-85]. Review of Thiessen 1981. Philippine Journal of Linguistics 15(2)-16(1): 109-111, at p. 109.
new_statements.locator: Zorc review p. 109, second full paragraph; quoting Thiessen 1981 p. 10
new_statements.rule_in_words: Thiessen (first-hand, but reached only through Zorc's quotation) says word accent in Canipaan/Southwest Palawano, like Quezon, Brooke's Point and Molbog, is non-contrastive and falls on the penult or the ultima; he does not say which, nor what conditions the choice. Zorc infers either a dialect-specific fixed position (ultima in some, penult in others) or unpredictable placement, and holds that Proto-Palawan lost the Proto-Philippine accent contrast.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Canipaan. Zorc notes Warren's Palawan-Batak minimal pairs (dáto/dató, dúduq/dudúq) contradict Thiessen for Batak, and that in his own Aborlan/Brooke's Point/Batak data accent differences are Tagalog or Bisayan superstratum effects varying by idiolect.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: 'word accent... of a word, including both suffixed and unsuffixed forms'; Thiessen pools four varieties (Quezon = Central Palawano, Brooke's Point, Canipaan = Southwest Palawano, Molbog) in one sentence. Zorc's reading is that dialects differ (some ultima-final, some penult) or that accent is sporadic; he does not say which pattern Canipaan has.
new_statements.identity_note: Thiessen's 'Canipaan' variety is Southwest Palawano [plv] (hh.bib lgcode 'Canipaan Palawan = Southwest Palawano [plv]'; Glottolog places sout2916 under 'Brooke-Canipaan Palawan', broo1240). The quoted accent statement is made jointly for Quezon (= Central Palawano [plc], cent2091), Brooke's Point Palawano [plw] (broo1239), Canipaan [plv] and Molbog [pwm], so it is not specific to plv. The sibling statement 'stress falls on the penultimate syllable' (Revel 1995; Revel-Macdonald 1979) concerns Central Palawano [plc] of the Brooke's Point highlands, not plv. The SIL 1974 Mararango/Candawaga wordlist (Rizal municipality) is probably plv territory but is unlabelled and carries no accent marks.

sources.citation: Revel, Nicole. 1995. Palawan. In Darrell T. Tryon (ed.), Comparative Austronesian Dictionary, Part 1 Fascicle 1, 351ff. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter. (Rosetta Project 2-page phonology excerpt)
sources.note: Sec. 2 iv 'Syllable structure and stress': 'Palawan syllables are of the form V, CV, VC, CVC Stress falls on the penultimate syllable.' Revel's Palawan is Central Palawano [plc] (Brooke's Point highlands, Makagwaq/Tamlang valleys), not plv; recorded here as a sibling-variety statement only.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1983c [publ. 1984-85]. Review of Thiessen, Henry Arnold, 1981, Phonological reconstruction of Proto-Palawan (Anthropological Papers 10, Manila: National Museum, 44 pp.). Philippine Journal of Linguistics 15(2)-16(1): 109-111.
sources.note: p. 109 quotes Thiessen 1981:10 verbatim: word accent in Quezon, Brooke's Point, Canipaan and Molbog 'falls on one of the last two syllables of a word, including both suffixed and unsuffixed forms... In none of the languages are words distinguished by accent alone so accent is not contrastive on this level and is not written'. Zorc reads this as either some dialects oxytone / some paroxytone, or accent sporadic and unpredictable; from his own Aborlan, Brooke's Point and Batak data he thinks Proto-Palawan lost PPH accent and present contrasts are Tagalog/Bisayan mimicry.
